idiom_name: std::sync::Weak<T> / std::rc::Weak<T> with Arc::downgrade and upgrade() -> Option<Arc<T>>
implementation_notes: Rust's standard library provides the non-owning edge as Weak<T>: Arc::downgrade(&arc) (or Rc::downgrade) creates it, upgrade() returns Option<Arc<T>> -> None once the value has been dropped, and Arc::new_cyclic gives a value a Weak pointer to itself during construction for self-referential graphs. Ownership discipline does the rest: Rc/Arc cycles leak because the strong count never reaches zero, so the documented fix is to make one edge of the cycle Weak - the canonical shape for child-to-parent back-references and observer registries. Weak keeps the allocation alive but not the value, and it offers no notification hook, so cleanup belongs in the strongly owning side's Drop.
pitfalls: upgrade() fails exactly when the last strong owner dropped: treat None as a normal path and never unwrap it in a loop over weakly held children unless liveness is guaranteed elsewhere.
Rc/Weak are neither Send nor Sync, so moving a weak edge to another thread requires Arc/Weak with T: Send + Sync - and mixing the two families for one value creates two independent allocations.
Weak keeps the allocation alive while any Weak exists (the value is already dropped and cannot be resurrected), so a long-lived Vec<Weak<T>> pins memory just as a weak_ptr registry does.
There is no notification callback: cleanup lives in Drop of the strong owner, and the upgrade-versus-last-drop race is not something the compiler reminds you to handle.
